methods.label: Use the equilateral triangle, then a midpoint
methods.explanation:
First use the equilateral triangle to determine the angle at \(A\). Let
\[
\alpha=\angle BAE=\angle ACD.
\]
Because \(F\) lies on \(CD\) and \(E\) lies on \(BC\), the equilateral triangle gives \(\angle DCE=60^\circ\). Hence \(\angle ACE=\alpha+60^\circ\). Also, \(F\) lies on segment \(AE\), so rays \(EF\) and \(EA\) coincide, giving \(\angle AEC=60^\circ\). The angle sum in \(\triangle ACE\) now gives
\[
\angle CAE=180^\circ-(\alpha+60^\circ)-60^\circ=60^\circ-\alpha.
\]
Since \(AE\) lies inside angle \(BAC\),
\[
\angle BAC=\alpha+(60^\circ-\alpha)=60^\circ.
\]

The relation \(AB=2AC\) suggests taking the midpoint \(M\) of \(AB\). Then \(AM=MB=AC\). Triangle \(AMC\) has two equal sides with included angle \(60^\circ\), so its other two angles are also \(60^\circ\); it is equilateral.

Consequently, \(MC=MB\), and the opposite rays \(MA\) and \(MB\) give \(\angle CMB=120^\circ\). The two base angles of isosceles triangle \(MCB\) are therefore
\[
\angle MCB=\angle CBM=\frac{180^\circ-120^\circ}{2}=30^\circ.
\]
Thus
\[
\angle ACB=\angle ACM+\angle MCB=60^\circ+30^\circ=90^\circ.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{90^\circ}\), choice \(\boxed{\text{C}}\).
